en: The Ritual Text for the Bodhisattva Precepts,
Spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty.
Expounded by the Bodhisattva disciple Zhixu.
This text is extracted from the "Chapter on Ethics" within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
All who receive the Bodhisattva precepts should know this most thoroughly; therefore, Master Xuanzang translated it as a separate work. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi*:

The treatise consists of one hundred fascicles, divided into five sections: first, the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section); second, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on Compendium of Determinations); third, the *Vyākhyāsaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on Compendium of Explanations);

fourth, the *Paryāyasaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on Compendium of Synonyms); and fifth, the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on Compendium of Subjects). Within the first, the *Maulī Bhūmi*, it is further divided into seventeen stages (*bhūmi*):

first, the *Pañcavijñānakāyasamprayuktā Bhūmi* (Stage Associated with the Five Groups of Consciousness); second, the *Manobhūmi* (Mind Stage); and third, the *Savitarkā Savicārā Bhūmi* (Stage with Vitarka and Vicāra).
1. The stage [of the desire realm]. 2. The stage of the form realm. 3. The stage of the formless realm. 4. The stage with vitarka and vicāra. 5.
The stage without vitarka and with only vicāra. 6. The stage without vitarka and without vicāra. 7. The stage of meditative equipoise (samāhita). 8. The stage not in meditative equipoise.

9. The stage with mind. 10. The stage without mind. 11. The stage consisting of what is heard (śrutamaya). 12. The stage consisting of what is reflected upon (cintāmaya). 13. The stage consisting of what is cultivated (bhāvanāmaya).
The stages to be accomplished (*abhisamaya-bhūmi*). Thirteenth is the stage of the śrāvaka (*śrāvaka-bhūmi*); fourteenth is the stage of the pratyekabuddha (*pratyekabuddha-bhūmi*);
fifteenth is the stage of the bodhisattva (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*); sixteenth is the stage with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*); seventeenth is the stage without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-bhūmi*).
Within the fifteenth, the stage of the bodhisattva, there are further divided four sections (*dhāraṇī*). Within the first section, there are divided eighteen chapters (*varga*). The tenth...

The Chapter on Precepts (*Śīla-varga*). Both the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* and the *Karmavācanā* texts are entirely derived from this [work]. As for the term "bodhisattva," in the Sanskrit language it is fully called *bodhisattva*;
this translates as "enlightened sentient being" (*jue youqing*). This means that one is able to give rise to great wisdom and great compassion:
through wisdom, one seeks the Buddha-way above; through compassion, one transforms sentient beings below. Furthermore, even if one were to lack great compassion...
Then one will not achieve the path of Buddhahood. If one lacks great wisdom, it is difficult to deliver sentient beings.

When compassion and wisdom are practiced together, and compassion and wisdom are non-dual, one is therefore called a Bodhisattva. There are three aggregates of precepts (*śīla-skandha*): first, the precept of restraining from unwholesome conduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), wherein no evil is left unrestrained;

second, the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), wherein no good is left unpracticed; third, the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*). Furthermore...
This is called the "precept of gathering sentient beings," for there is no birth that it does not deliver. In Sanskrit, it is *karma*;

it may be translated as "performing rites," "accomplishing tasks," or "action. Seeking its meaning, it refers to performing formal procedures (*vidhi*) before the assembly to accomplish matters in accordance with the Dharma.
The text is divided into three parts: first, the *karma* for receiving the precepts; second, the *karma* for repenting offenses; [and third, the *karma* for ordination].
II. The Third [Section]: The Distinction Between Attaining and Relinquishing.
The First [Sub-section]: The *Karmavācanā* for Receiving Precepts. This is further divided into two parts: first, receiving from a preceptor; second, receiving before an image.
Within the first part, there are four sections: first, the formal announcement requesting witness; second, the actual conferral of the precepts; third...
The conclusion of the ritual. Fourth, the examination of those who are not suitable vessels. This consists of two parts: first, seeking permission;
second, the formal announcement. The first part also has two sections: first, the request; second, the granting of permission. Now, the first [the request].
If bodhisattvas— whether householders or those who have gone forth— desire to train in the three clusters of pure precepts of a bodhisattva,
they should first generate the great aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and then diligently seek out fellow bodhisattvas who practice the same Dharma.
Having already made the great vow, being wise and powerful, and capable of bestowing and elucidating the meaning expressed through speech—
one should first prostrate at the feet of such a superior Bodhisattva endowed with these virtues, bare the right shoulder, and place the kneecaps upon the ground.

With palms joined in reverence, he makes this request: "Venerable sir, please take heed. I, who am named [so-and-so], beg you, venerable sir, to grant me the reception of all the pure precepts of a bodhisattva.
I pray that you will, out of compassion, deign to grant them to me for a moment, without regarding the fatigue."

The second and third times were also spoken in this manner. Having thus made this unerring request, he bared his right shoulder, paid respectful homage, and made offerings to the World-Honored Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, as well as to the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages, attained great wisdom, and acquired great supernormal powers.
He focused his mind exclusively on their various merits before him, giving rise to a profound...
The pure mind—the jewel of the bodhicitta—is inherent to all people. Once one resolves to seek the precepts, they are then called a Bodhisattva.
Having become a Bodhisattva, one must study the Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-vidha-śīla*). To study these precepts, it is logically necessary to formally receive them; for this reason alone...
These grave and light precepts, being able to cease evil, naturally possess all manner of virtues; being able to restrain oneself, they are likewise able to sustain all living beings.
Therefore, they are called the Threefold Pure Precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*). These precepts apply to both the laity and the ordained;
however, one must first give rise to a great vow as their foundation before being fit to receive them. If one does not give rise to a great vow, [one cannot receive them].

Even if one seeks to receive [the precepts], one will not obtain them. Having made the vow to seek and receive them, one must carefully investigate and seek out fellow Bodhisattvas of the same Dharma.

"Carefully" means seeking with precision and detail; "investigating" means seeking with thoroughness and urgency. This is because if one does not exercise care, there is a fear of returning to one who is not a true teacher;
if one does not investigate, there is a fear of losing a virtuous guide. What is meant by "fellow Dharma" refers to those who are... [as previously mentioned].
I have attained that which my heart agrees with: the desire to seek the Way above and transform those below. If one does not share this same Dharma, how could they be fit to act as a teacher?
Furthermore, although one has already made the Great Vow, one must further possess wisdom; only then will one know for oneself how to apply the Dharma.
If one possesses power, one can bestow it upon others; if one is able to transmit and elucidate the meaning expressed through words, then one relies on the meaning rather than the words.
Thus, one can respond according to the faculties of others and answer according to their dispositions. Only one who is endowed with such superior merits may serve as a teacher.
Once a teacher has been found, one must earnestly request instruction through the three karmas, beginning by prostrating at his feet.
Baring one shoulder and kneeling on the knees expresses the utmost reverence. Joining the palms expresses a mind directed toward no other object;
these all constitute the purity of bodily action (*kāyakarman*). The two words "reverence" (*gongjing*) constitute the purity of mental goodness (*manaḥ-kuśala*).

Such phrases as the words of invitation constitute the purity of verbal action (*vākkarman*). As for why the words of invitation must be spoken three times: two would not be earnest enough, while four would be excessive.

It would be too cumbersome; therefore, one recites only three times, which is called the "middle way. When the three types of action are all pure and the request is made according to the Dharma, it is called a "non-perverted request.
After having made the request, one again pays homage and makes offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the phrase "recalling those merits and giving rise to a profound, reverent, and pure mind":
by means of these bodhisattva precepts, one takes all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the entire Dharma-realm as one's teachers and witnesses.

Once received, all Buddhas of the ten directions are one's teachers, and all Bodhisattvas of the great earth are one's fellow students. Only when one gives rise to such a mind can it truly be called [the bodhisattva precepts].

Only when one is profoundly earnest can it be called "pure. "Great Earth" refers to the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) up to the Stage of Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), as extensively elucidated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures.
Second, the permission:

When bodhisattvas wish to confer the bodhisattva precepts upon another bodhisattva, they should first explain the Bodhisattva-piṭaka-mātṛkā—the bodhisattva training rules (*śikṣāpada*) and the characteristics of transgressions—causing them to hear and receive it. They should...
With wisdom, one observes one's own inclinations; one must be capable of reflecting and discerning before receiving the bodhisattva precepts.
It should be known that one who does not receive them merely because of another’s exhortation, nor for the sake of surpassing others, is called a firm bodhisattva.
Being worthy of receiving the bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), one should correctly bestow it according to the ritual for receiving the precepts as appropriate.
When a disciple seeks a teacher, they must investigate thoroughly; likewise, when a teacher takes a disciple under their care, they must also be careful and prudent.
*Mātṛkā* means "Mother" (or "Source"); it excellently explains the characteristics and meanings of all phenomena and is similar to the *Abhidharma*.
The *Mātṛkā* can give rise to sublime wisdom (*prajñā*), and sublime wisdom arises because of this treatise (*śāstra*); therefore, they are both successively termed "Wisdom Treatises. Bodhi...

The "Śikṣāpada" refers to the various precepts, both grave and light. The "offense-locus" refers to the fact that among these precepts, there are those whose transgression is defiled and those whose transgression is undefiled.
If one must conduct such an examination even when someone else comes to request ordination, then the gravity of the matter can be known.
Now, as for those who recklessly urge others to receive the precepts—do they not reflect upon this even slightly?

The second [section] consists of three parts concerning the formal announcement (*jñapti*). First, the announcement by the seeker of ordination; second, the announcement by the bestower of the Dharma; third, the clarification of the benefits obtained.

Within the first [of these], there are again three sub-sections: first, the ritual for the announcement; second, the words of the announcement; third, the purification of the mind following the announcement.
First: The bodhisattva receiving the precepts, moreover, before a wise and powerful superior bodhisattva, with humility and reverence,
kneeling with his kneecaps on the ground and joining his palms before an image of the Buddha, makes this request:
Second is the formal request for permission.
"I pray that the Virtuous One, out of compassion, will bestow upon me the Bodhisattva pure precepts.
The previous instance was a private request before the teacher; this is now the formal request before the image. As for the requirement to state the private request three times:
The teacher has not yet granted permission; this is because one must be solemn and respectful. When requesting the formal instruction, it is said only once, so as not to weary or trouble the teacher.
After the three recitations, one purifies the mind.
Having made this request, he focused his mind on a single object, cultivating a pure heart.
Thinking, "I shall before long attain the inexhaustible, immeasurable, and unsurpassed treasury of great merit," he remained silent, dwelling in contemplation of the meaning of these matters.

The single object is the present objective sphere of receiving the precepts. The pure mind is the mind that seeks the precepts. The *saṃgrahavastu-śīla* (precept of gathering sentient beings) is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*);
it is called the inexhaustible treasury of great merit. The *kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas) is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā-guṇa*);
it is called the immeasurable treasury of great merit. The *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint) is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*); it is called the [inexhaustible]...
It is the supreme treasury of great merit. Furthermore, because the one aggregate is the three aggregates, it is inexhaustible; because the three aggregates are the one aggregate, it is immeasurable.
It is most honored and most noble; because it is inconceivable, it is unsurpassed.
There are two parts to the formal announcement by the one who bestows the Dharma, and each of these has two sub-parts: first, the inquiry; second, the formal announcement. Regarding the first:
at that time, a wise and powerful bodhisattva, with an undistracted mind, [addresses] that bodhisattva who is capable of practicing the correct conduct.
Whether sitting or standing, he should speak these words: "Listen, son of good family named so-and-so.
Are you a bodhisattva? He should reply, "I am. "Have you made the vow for awakening? He should reply, "I have already made it. From this point forward...
One should speak as follows: "Listen, son of good family named so-and-so.
You now wish to receive from me all the training precepts of the bodhisattvas and all the pure ethical disciplines of the bodhisattvas, namely, the discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*)."
The precept of gathering virtuous dharmas and the precept of benefiting sentient beings— such training rules and such pure ethics were already possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past,
will be possessed by all bodhisattvas of the future, and are currently possessed by all bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions of the present.
Regarding these training rules and these pure ethics, all bodhisattvas of the past have already...
"Study! All bodhisattvas of the future shall study; all bodhisattvas of the present are now studying. Can you receive this?
He replied, "I can receive it. The bodhisattva who bestows [the precepts] spoke thus a second and a third time.
The bodhisattva who receives likewise answered thus a second and a third time.
One who is free from a distracted mind observes with right wisdom and accords with the bodhicitta;
thus they are able to seal the mind with the mind, rather than merely reciting words and phrases with the mouth. Within this, there are three rounds of question and answer:
first, one must directly accept the name of "Bodhisattva" without giving rise to retreat or discouragement; second, one must truly generate the bodhicitta.
The vow is not merely a hollow name; it must be truly real in three respects: one must be able to receive and study the Threefold Pure Precepts (Tri-śaraṇa-śīla).
It is not merely an empty aspiration. As for the first two question-and-answer sessions, they are conducted only once because the intent is already determined.
As for the third question-and-answer session, it requires three repetitions because of the need for thorough and careful examination.
Second, the formal announcement.
Having thus received [the precepts], the receiving Bodhisattva does not rise from their seat.

The conferring Bodhisattva, before the Buddha image, pays respectful homage and makes offerings to all Buddhas currently dwelling throughout the ten directions, as well as to all Bodhisattvas, prostrating at their feet.
He makes this formal declaration: "I prostrate to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions.
Now, within these realms, there is a bodhisattva named [Name] who, in my presence as [Name] Bodhisattva, has received the bodhisattva precepts up to three times.
I act as his witness. I pray that you, throughout the infinite and boundless worlds of the ten directions..."

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the foremost true sages, who have attained manifest awakening regarding all sentient beings at all times and in all places—whether manifest or unmanifest—also act as witnesses for this Bodhisattva named [Name], who has received the precepts. A second and a third time.
It is also explained in this way:
the recipient of the bodhisattva vows does not rise from their seat; that is, they remain kneeling as before while listening to the formal announcement (*jñapti*) of the bestower.
These three announcements constitute the *karmavācanā* for the conferral of the precepts. When the first *karmavācanā* is completed, throughout the worlds of the ten directions...
The sublime and virtuous precepts of the dharmadhātu, through the power of the mental karma, are all made to tremble.

At the conclusion of the second *karmavācanā*, the sublime and virtuous precepts of the dharmadhātu throughout the worlds of the ten directions are like clouds and canopies, covering the crown of the recipient’s head.

At the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*, the sublime and virtuous precepts of the dharmadhātu throughout the worlds of the ten directions flow from the crown aperture of the recipient into their body and mind, filling them completely.
The response: "Until the end of the future, may you forever serve as the seed of the Buddha.
Thus, its benefits are clarified.
When the ritual for receiving the precepts (*karmavācanā*) has thus been completed, immediately thereafter, throughout the infinite and boundless ten directions...
Before all the Buddhas currently residing in various worlds and before the bodhisattvas who have already entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*), a natural mark (*dharmatā-nimitta*) appears.
By this, it is indicated that such a bodhisattva has received the pure precepts undertaken by bodhisattvas.
At that time, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas of the ten directions observe this natural mark of the bodhisattva and, because they give rise to mindfulness, they possess correct knowledge and vision.

Furthermore, by means of right knowledge and vision, one truly realizes that in a certain world, a bodhisattva of such-and-such a name, in the presence of a certain bodhisattva, has correctly received the pure precepts of a bodhisattva.

Toward all those bodhisattvas who have received these precepts, one generates a sense of affection and kindness, regarding them as a son or a younger brother, and cherishes them with compassion. Through the compassionate mindfulness of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, this [person] is...
The Bodhisattva seeks the wholesome dharmas, which increase all the more and never diminish. This is called the formal announcement and request for witness when receiving the Bodhisattva precepts.
The nature of the mind of this present moment has, from the beginning, been vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive.

Now, by being able to give rise to the bodhicitta in accordance with this nature and receiving the Bodhisattva precepts, one’s mind becomes perfectly fused and identical with that of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, as soon as the *karmavācanā* ceremony is completed, it is natural that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will know, see, and even take one into their compassionate remembrance.
Through compassionate empowerment, may their progress be further increased. Such is the inconceivable nature of the mutual resonance between the path and its response.
How is it that the masses, lost in delusion, do not resolve to awaken? This concludes the initial petition for witness.

The second [section], the method for the formal bestowal of the precepts, has four parts: first, clarifying the characteristics of the precepts; second, clarifying the characteristics of transgressions; third, distinguishing them from the Hīnayāna;

and fourth, concluding with a praise of their superior merit. The first part [of the four] further has three sections: first, the heading and inquiry; second, the detailed explanation; and third, the conclusion. Now, the first [of these three].
If Bodhisattvas abide in the ethical discipline of restraint (*śīla-saṃvara*), there are four types of defeat (*pārājika*) dharmas. What are these four? Regarding the dharma of defeat:
wisdom is "self" and afflictions (*kleśa*) are "other"; the Buddha-dharma is "self" and the power of Māra is "other.
Having generated the resolve and received the Bodhisattva precepts, they originally intended to subdue the armies of Māra and destroy the thieves of affliction; yet now...
If one violates this precept, one will instead be overcome by afflictions and likewise overcome by the power of Māra.

Now, although the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* fully elucidates the ten grave precepts (*daśa-guru-dharma*), only the latter four are listed here for three reasons. First, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are termed the "fundamental precepts" (*mūla-śīla*).
Regardless of whether one is a layperson or a monastic—be they a śrāmaṇera or a bhikṣu—if one wishes to receive [the full ordination], [these must be observed].

Regarding this Bodhisattva precept: one must have already previously received the five precepts, the ten precepts, the full ordination (*upasampadā*), and so forth; what need is there to labor over proclaiming them again?
Now, we merely clarify the superior propagation [of the Dharma] above and the transformative guidance below, as well as the enhanced discipline (*adhiśīla*).

Second, as for the fundamental precept-dharmas, even if those among the seven assemblies (*saptasaṃgha*) should commit an offense, repentance is not permitted; even if the Mahāyāna allows for such repentance, [the gravity of the offense remains].
One must observe auspicious signs. Regarding these four precepts: if they are violated through bonds of weak or medium intensity, it is sufficient to perform repentance and purification;
however, if they are violated through bonds of superior intensity, re-ordination remains permissible. Therefore, these cannot be conflated with the fundamental four precepts.
Third, regarding the conduct of a bodhisattva: whether following or contrary [to worldly norms], there are many skillful means (*upāya*).

Thus, for killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, there may be instances where they are permitted or prohibited. However, these four precepts must never be transgressed in any place or within any realm of existence;
therefore, they alone are clearly elucidated here.
The second part, the detailed explanation, consists of four sections. The first concerns praising oneself and disparaging others regarding their ethical discipline.
If a bodhisattva, out of a desire to seek gain and honor, praises themselves and disparages others, this is called the first *pārājika* offense.

Anger and disparagement are still relatively light; greed for praise is grave. To practice both praise and disparagement together causes others to distance themselves from one and become attached to oneself—how could this be the mind of a bodhisattva?
Second is stinginess regarding wealth, the Dharma, and the precepts.
If a bodhisattva, despite possessing wealth and resources, fails to give rise to compassion and practice wise relinquishment when those who are suffering,
impoverished, without refuge, and without protection come before him seeking wealth— because of a naturally stingy disposition toward material things— then this seeker of the Dharma [is deprived].
When it manifests before one, because of an inherent stinginess regarding the Dharma, one does not relinquish or give away the Dharma even though it is currently available.
This is called the second *parājika* offense.

Bestowing both material wealth and the Dharma is the primary duty of a bodhisattva; this refers to having material resources currently at hand, distinguishing this from being without resources, as one who is impoverished and suffering has none.
O Protector! To distinguish those who should not be solicited and yet fail to give to them is to be utterly devoid of wisdom.
To diligently practice giving for the sake of Bodhi, without dwelling on signs, is called "wisdom-giving. Regarding one who correctly seeks the Dharma:
to distinguish those who do not seek it, and even when the Dharma is present, to distinguish those who lack it—if one does not relinquish this, what is the use of claiming to know the Dharma?
The third is the precept against harboring anger and refusing to accept repentance.
If a bodhisattva nurtures such a form of the fetter of resentment, for this reason, they do not merely initiate harsh speech and then desist;
rather, being obscured by anger, they further employ hands, feet, clods of earth, stones, knives, or staves to strike, beat, injure, or harm others.
To cause harm and affliction to sentient beings; to harbor within oneself an intention of fierce anger and resentment;
when having committed an offense, to refuse and fail to endure the apologies and admonitions of others, and to not relinquish the bond of enmity—this is called the third *parājika* dharma.
When a single thought of anger arises, a million gates of obstruction open; how much more so when one beats or harms others?
How much more so when one performs repentance yet still does not accept it? Since one has already severed ties with sentient beings, where is the power of the vow for Bodhi?
The fourth is the teaching on the precept against similitude-dharma.
If any bodhisattvas slander the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and instead delight in proclaiming, elucidating, and establishing similitude-to-the-true-dharma.
Regarding the counterfeit Dharma, whether one has confidence and understanding in it oneself or follows the lead of others, this is called the fourth *pārājika* offense.
The true, authentic Dharma is definitively consistent with the single seal and the three seals;
the counterfeit Dharma, however, appears to be so but is not—it is definitively consistent with the two nets of craving and views. To speak of such a counterfeit Dharma is itself termed "slander."
Regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, it is not necessarily the case that one slanders the Dharma only by rejecting and disparaging it.

Since it has already been in circulation for a long time, to raise it up once again is called "proclaiming"; to expound, expand, support, and assist it so as to cause it to increase and broaden is called "revealing."
To innovate one's own discourse and separately set forth a distinct tenet is called "establishment" (*pratisthāpana*). To be self-confident in one's own understanding is to be a false teacher;

to follow others is to be a false disciple. If one cannot distinguish between the false and the correct, then all who propagate the Dharma are in fact slanderers of the Dharma. Is this not to be lamented?
These three constitute the completion [of the offense]. Thus are called the four kinds of *parājika* dharmas for a bodhisattva.
That they are termed "bodhisattva *parājika*" precisely indicates that they are not shared with the Hīnayāna. If one kills, steals, or...
Sexual misconduct and false speech are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and are termed the "root precepts. The first section, clarifying the characteristics of the precepts, is concluded.
The second section, clarifying the characteristics of transgressions, has two parts: first, the manifestation of faults; second, the distinctions. Now, the first part begins.
If a bodhisattva commits even one of these four defeats (*pārājika*), let alone all of them,
they will no longer be capable of increasing and gathering the vast provisions for enlightenment within this present life,
nor will they be capable of purifying their intention (*āśaya*) in this present life. Such a person is called a "semblance bodhisattva," not a true bodhisattva.
"Committing one of the four" means committing any one among the four types of offenses. "How much more so for committing all" means committing all four types.
"The present life" refers to this current single lifetime. "Vast provisions for enlightenment" refers to the six perfections, the myriad practices, and so forth.
"Pure intention" refers to the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Pure Mind (*śuddhādhyāśaya-bhūmi*).
Second, the distinction:

if a bodhisattva violates the four types of defeats (pārājika) through weak or middling grades of entanglement (paryavasthāna), they do not relinquish the bodhisattva’s vow of pure ethical discipline (śīla-saṃvara).
However, if they violate them through a superior grade of entanglement, it is termed "relinquishment. Thus, if bodhisattvas violate the four types...
If one repeatedly practices the offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*), being entirely devoid of shame and dread of blame, deeply delighting in them and perceiving them as meritorious qualities,
it should be known that this is called an offense of superior entanglement (*adhimātra-paryavasthāna*).

The *paryavasthānas* (envelopments) are ten: first, anger; second, concealment; third, drowsiness; fourth, torpor; fifth, restlessness; sixth, regret; seventh, envy; eighth, avarice; ninth, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*); and tenth, lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*).

Each of these has three grades: inferior, middling, and superior. "Soft" refers to the inferior grade. Committing an offense while under the influence of the inferior or middling grades of the ten *paryavasthānas* does not constitute a loss of the precepts.
However, committing an offense while under the influence of the superior grade of the *paryavasthānas* constitutes a loss of the precepts.

"Abandoning" means losing [the precepts]. From "frequently manifesting" onwards, there is a re-explanation of the characteristics of committing an offense through superior-grade entanglements (*paryavasthāna*). Part two concludes the explanation of the characteristics of offenses.
Part three distinguishes this from the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). First, it explains what is not lost; second, it explains that even after loss, restoration is possible. Now...
First, it is not the case that a bodhisattva relinquishes the bodhisattva’s vow of pure ethical discipline merely by once manifesting an act that constitutes a defeat (pārājika),
as is the case for a bhikṣu who, upon committing an act of defeat, immediately abandons the prātimokṣa vows.
"Bhikṣu" is the same as "bhikṣu"; they differ only in their Sanskrit pronunciation (*bhaṣṭa* vs. *bhāṣya*). The precepts of a bhikṣu rely exclusively on external conditions;
therefore, they are easily lost. The precepts of a bodhisattva are induced by the bodhicitta; therefore, they are difficult to lose.

Furthermore, the *pārājika* offenses for a bhikṣu—namely, sexual misconduct, theft, killing, and lying—result in the permanent loss [of the precepts] upon a single transgression. As for the *pārājika* offenses of a bodhisattva...
The Dharma is that which destroys stinginess, anger, and slander; therefore, even if one commits an offense incidentally, it is not yet lost.
Regarding the Prātimokṣa—its Sanskrit name is *Prātimokṣa*—the second point clarifies that once it has been lost, it can still be received again.
If bodhisattvas, through such a transgression, abandon the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), they remain capable of receiving it again in this very life;
they are not incapable, unlike a bhikṣu who, while abiding in the prātimokṣa vows, commits an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*).
In this present life, one is no longer capable of receiving [the precepts] again due to such transgression;
this refers to a violation committed with a superior degree of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*). Even if the precepts are lost, it is still permitted to receive them again;
therefore, this differs from the Hīnayāna. Furthermore, it should be understood that by means of a superior degree of entanglement, one commits these violations: stinginess, anger, and slander.
Regarding the four precepts: one merely loses the Bodhisattva precepts but does not lose the Bhikṣu precepts; therefore, one performs repentance and remains eligible to receive them again.

However, if one violates the four precepts of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, then one has lost both the Bhikṣu precepts and the Bodhisattva precepts and is no longer eligible to receive them.
Even if one relies on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* for repentance and attains a favorable sign, one is permitted only to act as a Bodhisattva.
A *sāmanera* upāsaka may become a bodhisattva *śrāmaṇera*, but he can never become a bodhisattva *bhikṣu*.
This concludes the third section, which distinguishes [the Mahāyāna] from the Hīnayāna.
Fourth, the conclusion and praise of the excellence of its merit, in two parts: first, clarifying its superiority; second, illustrating it by analogy. Now, the first part.
The pure ethical discipline thus undertaken by a bodhisattva is the most excellent and supreme among all other forms of pure ethical discipline;
it is accompanied by an immeasurable and boundless treasury of great merit, is initiated by the foremost and most sublime virtuous mental disposition,
and is universally capable of eliminating every kind of evil conduct of all sentient beings.

All other forms of received pure precepts—referring to the eight precepts, the five precepts, the ten precepts, the full precepts, and so forth—none of these various pure precepts fail to flow forth from the ocean of the Bodhisattva’s pure precepts, nor do they fail to return to that ocean of the Bodhisattva’s pure precepts.
Therefore, this precept alone is the most excellent and supreme; this is the general praise.
It is followed by a great treasury of merit; it praises the supreme benefits thereby obtained. It is originated by the foremost of intentions;
it praises the superior mind on the causal ground. It is capable of universally eliminating all unwholesome conduct; it praises its supreme power to extinguish transgressions.
This is illustrated by two examples:
all the prātimokṣa vows do not equal even one hundredth part of this bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline;
they do not equal one thousandth part, nor a numerical fraction, nor a calculable fraction, nor a fractional part, nor a metaphorical fraction, nor even an upaniṣad fraction thereof.
It does not even equal one [fraction]. This is because it encompasses all great merits.
"All *pratimokṣa* vows" refers here to everything from the eight precepts up to the full set of monastic precepts.
*Upaniṣad* is translated here as "near" or "slight. This means that a minute particle (*paramāṇu*) is a near and slight portion of form. [End of] Major Section.
2. The formal conferral of the precepts is concluded.
3. Summary of the concluding ritual.
Having thus performed the *karmavācanā* and other matters for receiving the bodhisattva precepts, both the preceptor and the recipient arise together to perform offerings.
Throughout the boundless and limitless worlds of the ten directions, they prostrate at the feet of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and withdraw with reverence.
This concludes the formal announcement and request for witness; following the actual conferral of the precepts, one should each direct the mind universally.
This is the offering.
Second, the discernment of those who are not suitable vessels has two parts: first, not receiving [the precepts] from them; second, not teaching them. Regarding the first:
furthermore, bodhisattvas do not seek to receive the pure bodhisattva precepts from all those who are merely clever or wise.

One who lacks pure faith should not receive [the precepts] from such a person; that is, one who has no initial faith or understanding regarding the pure ethical discipline thus received, who is unable to enter into it, and who does not engage in proper reflection.
Furthermore, one who possesses stinginess and greed, one who is obscured by stinginess and greed, or one who has great desire [should not be a teacher].

One should not receive [the precepts] from one who lacks contentment; nor from one who has violated the pure precepts, who lacks reverence for the various points of training, or who is lax and negligent regarding the restraint of the precepts;
nor from one who harbors anger and resentment, or who is largely intolerant.
One should not receive [the precepts] from one who is unable to endure the transgressions of others;

nor from one who is indolent, or one who is lazy, who for the most part is attached to sleep day and night, who delights in reclining, who delights in lying down, who delights in associating with crowds, or who delights in idle chatter.
Nor should one receive them from one whose mind is distracted, such that they cannot maintain a single moment of virtuous thought for even as long as it takes to milk a cow.
Regarding those who practice while remaining in dependence: one should not receive [the teachings] from them.

One should not receive them from those who are obscured by darkness, those of a deluded nature, those with extremely inferior minds, or those who slander the Bodhisattva-piṭaka-sūtras and the mātṛkās.

This clarifies that a Bodhisattva Dharma teacher must carefully examine the capacity of the recipient. One must not recklessly comply with a person’s request and allow them to receive [the precepts] at will.
For these Bodhisattva pure precepts are sought and received only by those who are wise and discerning;
since such a person currently lacks pure faith and even goes so far as to slander the sūtras and śāstras, how could they possibly be fit to receive these precepts?
Yes. Within the text, twenty-two categories are briefly enumerated: first, lack of pure faith, which refers to being unable to enter [the path] and engaging in improper reflection;
second, stinginess and greed; third, the obscuration of precepts by the dominance of stinginess and greed; fourth, great desire.

Five: lack of contentment. Six: violating the pure precepts; that is, having transgressed any of the received eight, five, ten, or full precepts, failing to perform repentance until an auspicious sign is obtained constitutes an obstruction. Seven:
lack of respect for the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*). Eight: being lax and negligent; that is, even regarding the eight precepts up to the full precepts and so forth, one still does not...
1. Lack of reverence and being arrogant or lax; how can such a person be fit to receive this supreme, augmenting precept?
2. Possessing anger and resentment. 3. Having little forbearance. 4. Being unable to endure the transgressions of others.
5. Being indolent and lacking in vigor. 6. Being lazy and lacking in diligence. 7. Frequently being attached to worldly things. 8. Slothfulness and reclining.
16. Lying down; 17. Delighting in associating with the multitude; 18. Delighting in idle chatter; 19.
Distraction, being unable to concentrate the virtuous mind on a single object; 20. Obscurity; 21. Ignorance; 22. An extremely inferior mind; 23.
Slandering the sūtras and śāstras. Persons such as these are certainly unable to don the armor of the great vow and proceed toward [enlightenment].

Because they are directed toward Bodhi, one should not receive [the precepts] from any of them. "Què" (愨) is pronounced "gòu. "Taking the time it takes to milk a cow" clarifies that [the duration] is extremely brief.
*Sūtra* (素怛纜) is the same as *sūtra*; this is translated as "Kie-king" (契經). *Mātṛkā* (摩怛迦) is the same as *mātṛkā*, which explains and manifests the preceding text.
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* does not permit the selection of caste; yet the present text specifically requires such selection.
One must discern the faculties [of the recipient]; that these are established through mutual reflection and abbreviation must not be unknown.
Second, there are those for whom one does not preach.
Furthermore, although various bodhisattvas may have already fully received and maintained the ultimate dharma of the bodhisattva vow-observance (*śīla-saṃvara*),...
Yet, toward those sentient beings who revile the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and lack faith, one must never hastily proclaim or awaken them.
Why is this? Because having heard it, they would be unable to believe or understand, being shrouded by the great obscuration of ignorance.

They will then give rise to slander. Because of that slander, just as one who abides in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline accomplishes a vast treasury of immeasurable merit, so too will that slanderer be pursued by a vast treasury of immeasurable sinful karma.
As long as all evil speech, evil views, and evil thoughts have not been permanently abandoned, one will ultimately not escape them.
When a Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, the priority lies in observing the capacities of the audience.

If they perceive that sentient beings can develop faith and delight in these pure precepts, they should proclaim and awaken them, causing them to give rise to the resolve to receive the precepts. Thus, the Brahmajāla Sūtra states:
This is not the precept of failing to transform sentient beings. However, one must certainly contemplate and examine the matter according to the circumstances;

how could one allow for hasty or reckless proclamation that would instead cause sentient beings to fall into sinful karma? One should know that those sutras and this treatise also mutually complement one another.
This concludes the first major section above, which clarifies receiving [the teachings] from a teacher.
Second, receiving [the precepts] before an image:
If a bodhisattva wishes to receive the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), yet does not encounter a person (*pudgala*) endowed with complete merit,
they should at that time personally receive the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline before an image of the Tathāgata.
One should receive [the vows] in this manner: baring the right shoulder, kneeling with the right knee on the ground, one should speak these words:
"I, who am named [so-and-so], respectfully address all Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the assembly of Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages.
I now desire, before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the worlds of the ten directions, to vow to receive all the bodhisattva training rules; I vow to receive all..."
The pure ethical discipline of a bodhisattva consists of the discipline of restraint, the discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the discipline of benefiting sentient beings.

Such points of training and such pure ethical discipline were fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the past, will be fully possessed by all bodhisattvas of the future, and are now fully possessed by all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions. Regarding these points of training and this pure ethical discipline...
Regarding the precepts: all bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in them; all bodhisattvas of the future shall train in them;
and all bodhisattvas currently existing throughout the ten directions are training in them now. The second and third [sections] are also spoken in this same way.
Having finished speaking, one should rise. All that remains should be understood as previously described.

A *pudgala*—translated here as "sentient being"—is one who is endowed with merit; that is, one who has already made the great vow, possesses wisdom and power, and is capable of bestowing and elucidating the meaning of the words.
If, after a thorough search, no such person can be found, only then may one permit self-ordination before an image.
If one encounters an enlightened master yet does not receive ordination from them, it is either due to ignorance or arrogance. This is the regulation of the Brahma Net Sūtra.
This instructs one to seek a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*). In this context, only the arousal of the bodhicitta is valued.

If people today wish to take the precepts through a self-vow, they must exercise great self-reflection. "I respectfully address the ten directions," and so forth, constitutes the text for the three *karmavācanās*.

All remaining matters should be understood as previously explained, namely: the manifestation of the natural characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) and the four grave offenses (*catur-uttara-pārājika*).
This concludes the first section on the *karmavācanā* for receiving the precepts.

The second section, the *Karma* for Confessing Faults, is further divided into two parts: first, the admonition not to commit transgressions; second, the procedure for confession should a transgression occur. Herein is the first part.
If bodhisattvas, having correctly received the code of discipline from another, do so with a motivation of seeking [the precepts] that is thoroughly pure, [they must maintain them].
With the intention for enlightenment and the intention to benefit all sentient beings, one should give rise to the utmost reverence and respect;
from the very beginning, one must apply oneself with diligence and not commit any transgression.

Whether before a preceptor or before an image, these are all termed "receiving from another. Regarding the *saṃvara-śīla* (morality of restraint), it is the intention of seeking training with complete purity;
regarding the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (morality of gathering virtuous dharmas), it is the *bodhicitta* intention;
and regarding the *sattva-anugrāhaka-śīla* (morality of benefiting sentient beings), it is the intention to benefit all sentient beings. From the very moment of receiving [the vows]...
Having done so, one should then remain single-mindedly and purely, constantly upholding and protecting these precepts so as not to transgress them;
by doing so, one will be fully endowed with the merits of the three clusters.
Second, regarding the confession of transgressions, there are two parts. First, a general admonition to eliminate them quickly; second, a specific demonstration of the two types of confession.
Now, for the first:
Should one commit a violation, one must immediately repent and eliminate it according to the Dharma, so as to restore purity.
If one commits an offense and does not repent, then evil and transgression will increase day and night; therefore, one should eliminate them as quickly as possible.
If one wishes to eliminate these offenses but cannot do so according to the Dharma, the offenses will likewise not be eliminated; thus, one is first cautioned to act in accordance with the Dharma.
It is like a clean garment that happens to be defiled by filth: it must be quickly washed with alkaline water before it can be restored to purity. One must not...

Regarding the ash-water: if the foul odor is not eliminated and it remains for many days, the stench will likewise be difficult to remove. Second, the specific presentation of the two types of repentance has two parts: first, repentance before another; second, self-vowed repentance. The first part also has two sections: first, clarifying the person against whom one repents; second, clarifying the distinctions in the methods of repentance. Now, the first section: The person against whom one repents refers to a fellow practitioner who is pure and upright, possessing the precepts and being free from transgressions. One must not approach someone who is impure, unrighteous, or lacking in virtue. Furthermore, one should not approach those who have committed grave offenses, such as the five heinous crimes or the four pārājika offenses, nor those who have abandoned the precepts, nor those who harbor malice toward the Three Jewels. One should instead seek out a virtuous companion who is capable of acting as a witness to the confession. This is because if one confesses before an unqualified person, the offense will not be purified, and one may even incur further transgression.

Therefore, one must carefully examine the character of the person against whom one repents. If they are truly pure and upright, then one’s own faults will be cleansed. This is called "repentance before another. It is like washing away filth with clean water; the more thorough the cleansing, the more the stains are removed. Thus, one should diligently seek out a worthy person to serve as a witness to one's confession. This concludes the first section.
It should be understood that all such transgressions by a bodhisattva are subsumed under *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
One should confess and repent them before a person of authority—one capable of understanding and receiving verbal expressions of action—who may belong to either the Śrāvaka or Mahāyāna vehicle.
"All transgressions" refers generally to the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*) within this context, as well as the forty-one minor offenses (*laghu-āpatti*) found in the *Prātimokṣa*.

The *bhikṣu* precepts are restricted to the monastic community (*saṃgha-cakra*); therefore, they are detailed in five sections (*pañca-varga*) and seven groups (*sapta-nikāya*), and are termed "secret teachings.
The Bodhisattva precepts apply to all seven classes of followers; therefore, all transgressions are uniformly termed "evil."
The performance [of the rite] is the same; there is only the distinction between what is subject to repentance and what is not, and whether it is light or grave.

One must receive the precepts from a Mahāyāna Dharma Master. Regarding repentance, there is no restriction as to whether it is Hīnayāna or Mahāyāna, because even a Hīnayāna bhikṣu is a member of the Saṃgha Jewel who is capable of extinguishing the transgressions of a Bodhisattva.

Second, the explanation of the distinctions in the methods of repentance has three parts: first, repenting for transgressions committed under the influence of superior-grade fetters; second, repenting for transgressions committed under the influence of middle-grade fetters;
and third, repenting for transgressions committed under the influence of inferior-grade fetters, as well as other violations. Now, the first part:

If a bodhisattva violates any of the aforementioned rules involving defeat (pārājika) through intense entanglements (adhimātra-paryavasthāna), they lose their moral discipline (śīla-saṃvara) and must receive it again.
The aforementioned rules involving defeat refer specifically to the four precepts concerning stinginess, anger, and slander. Therefore:
Although one who has lost the precepts is still permitted to receive them again, if one commits the offenses of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, or lying, one must seek to see auspicious signs.
This refers to the second method of repentance for violations involving middling-grade fetters.

If one commits an offense against any of these *pārājika* dharmas through a medium-grade entanglement (*madhyama-paryavasthāna*), one should, before three persons or more, perform the rite for the disclosure and removal of evil deeds (*pratikarman*). First, one should state the name of the offense committed.
One should speak thus: "Venerable one of focused mind," or "Great Virtue," "I, who am named so-and-so, have transgressed the Bodhisattva Vinaya rules as previously described [the specific matter].
I have committed an *āpatti* of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*). The remainder is as for a *bhikṣu*’s confession, repentance, and purification."
Regarding the procedure for the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing), it should be stated as follows:
"The rest is as for the bhikṣus," which should be said thus: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
I, [name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I now confess it before you, venerable sir; I shall not conceal it. Through confession there is peace; through non-confession there is not."
"I am not at ease. I recall my transgression and confess it. Knowing it, I do not conceal it.

Venerable sirs, please bear in mind that my body of pure precepts is intact and that I have fulfilled the pure Uposatha. Thus he should speak three times. They should say to him: "Reproach your own heart;
you should give rise to revulsion [for unwholesome states]. He should reply: "So be it. Furthermore, if one confesses before three persons, they...
Once the offender has arrived before the three sentient beings and confessed his transgression, one among these three who is to receive the confession should first ask the other two:
"If you, Elders, permit me to receive the confession of the bodhisattva [Name], I shall receive it. The two should respond, "So be it. Thereafter...
He accepts their confession. If one confesses before more than three persons, it constitutes a confession before the Saṃgha.

One should go into the midst of the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove one's shoes, prostrate at the feet of the monks, kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement: "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen."
"I, [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense. I now request the Saṃgha for confession. Thus he should say three times.

Among them, one who accepts the confession should make this formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This Bodhisattva [Name] has committed such-and-such an offense and now seeks confession from the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, and if the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, I shall accept [the confession] from [Name]."
The Bodhisattva’s Confession. Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made the announcement, the offender then presents the words of confession, up to:
“Speak and reproach your own mind; you should give rise to weary detachment. The offender replies, “So be it.”
Third, regarding the confession of down-grade entanglements and other transgressions:
if one has committed a transgression involving down-grade entanglements—such as the aforementioned defeats (*pārājika*) or other violations—one should confess before a single person (*pudgala*).
It should be understood that the method for this confession and repentance is the same as previously described.
The remaining transgressions refer to the forty-one minor offenses (*dukkaṭa*) within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*; they are also called "numerous offenses" and "light defilement sins.
This concludes the initial confession before another person.
Second is the confession through self-vow.

If there is no person of suitable character against whom one may openly disclose and repent of the transgression, the bodhisattva, with a pure intention, gives rise to a self-vowing thought: "I shall resolutely guard myself in the future and never commit it again."
In this way, regarding the emergence from and purification of transgressions,

one should follow a *pudgala*— that is, one who accords with the True Dharma of either the Hīnayāna or Mahāyāna and is capable of understanding and receiving verbal informative action (*vāgvijñapti*).
One should not confess to a person who has not received the precepts, nor should one [confess] toward...
If there are offenders who repent, then even if there are no pure persons of either the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna present, one may simply take a self-vow.
If this self-vow is made with sincere earnestness, then the transgression will depart and the precepts will be restored to purity. This concludes the second section:
the *karmavācanā* for the expiation of offenses.

The third section, on the distinctions regarding relinquishment, is further divided into two parts: first, clarifying the distinctions regarding the relinquishment of the vow; second, clarifying the distinctions regarding the acquisition of the vow. Now, for the first:

briefly, there are two conditions by which one relinquishes the bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*): first, the abandonment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Regarding the great vow for enlightenment: second, if one commits an offense that constitutes a defeat (*pārājika*) through the manifestation of intense fetters (*adhimātra-paryavasthāna*), one abandons the precepts;
this is the loss of the precepts. One receives the precepts only after first generating the great vow for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Now, since one has abandoned this vow, the precepts are likewise lost accordingly. This is the first condition. [The term] "intense fetters" refers to...

Committing an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*); these are the two conditions. However, if one has made a solemn vow or has repented and eliminated the offense according to the Dharma, it may still be received again.

Next, the distinctions regarding the attainment of the precepts are explained in two parts. First, the eternal attainment [of the precepts] until the end of the future is explained. (1) Explanation of the transformation.
This concerns the doubt regarding the reception [of the precepts] upon rebirth. First:

even if Bodhisattvas undergo a change of body throughout the worlds of the ten directions, in every place of birth they do not abandon the Bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*).
Because these Bodhisattvas have not abandoned their great vow for unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they likewise do not manifest [unwholesome conduct].
An offense involving the most severe entanglements constitutes a defeat (*pārājika*).
The Eight Precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*) are restricted to one day and night; the Five Precepts, Ten Precepts, and Full Ordination (*upasampadā*) are restricted to the duration of one’s life.
Only this Bodhisattva precept system, once obtained, is obtained forever, lasting until the end of the future. If not...
Regarding the two conditions for violating a grave precept through regressive thought, one ultimately does not abandon or lose them.
Second, the explanation of the transition to another birth and the doubt regarding the reception of gravity:
if various bodhisattvas transition to other births and forget their original resolve, they encounter virtuous friends who desire to awaken them.
Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, although one may receive them repeatedly, this is not a new reception, nor is it a new attainment.
Once the unmanifested (avijñapti) essence of the precepts has been generated, it becomes forever the seed of Buddhahood.

Even if one undergoes successive rebirths and forgets them, as long as there is no cause of regressive intent or the commission of a grave offense—these two conditions—the essence of the precepts should be known to remain, despite the fact that one receives them again and again.
It merely serves to bring about awakening; how could it be called "newly receiving" or "newly attaining"?
*Commentary on the Ritual Text for the Bodhisattva Precepts* (End).
